title: New in llama.cpp: Decision Models
gist: llama.cpp adds a /v1/systemone endpoint serving decision models that score user-supplied options with probabilities in one forward pass, with five open models from 144M to 27B parameters at 3-43 ms per question. Practical tips stress option descriptions and per-model confidence cutoffs.

themes.theme: Decision models as a new inference primitive

insights.claim: llama.cpp server now supports decision models via a /v1/systemone endpoint: the client sends a state (text, JSON or screenshot) plus typed questions and receives a probability for each option in a single forward pass.
insights.speaker: Xuan-Son Nguyen
insights.so_what: Local inference stacks are adding non-generative model serving; watch for adoption by routing/moderation tooling.

insights.claim: A decision model answers by scoring supplied options rather than generating text, so it avoids the one-forward-pass-per-output-token cost and the output parsing step of chat models, and its answer is always one of the given options with a probability attached.
insights.speaker: Xuan-Son Nguyen
insights.so_what: Cheaper, deterministic classification for agent routing, moderation and step verification can displace LLM calls in those workloads.
insights.quote: A decision model reads the input once, and its answer is always one of your options, with a probability attached.

insights.claim: Typical decision-model uses are routing requests, moderating content, checking that an agent's step worked, and choosing an agent's next action.
insights.speaker: Xuan-Son Nguyen
insights.so_what: Agent-infrastructure demand may shift toward small verifier/router models rather than large generators.

insights.claim: The API follows the System One format introduced with TypeSafe's Jev model, so existing clients only need a new base URL, and implementation is in llama.cpp PR #29818.
insights.speaker: Xuan-Son Nguyen
insights.so_what: A shared API format lowers switching costs across decision-model providers.

insights.claim: Responses report zero output tokens (example: 130 input tokens, 0 output tokens), showing decision models bill essentially only on input.
insights.speaker: Xuan-Son Nguyen
insights.so_what: Per-call cost structure differs sharply from generative LLMs, relevant to unit economics of high-volume classification.

insights.claim: The supported decision models range from 144M (Julia-1, mmBERT-small based, 50+ languages, 3 ms) to 27B parameters (OpenJev, Qwen3.8-27B based, 43 ms median per question on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000).
insights.speaker: Xuan-Son Nguyen
insights.so_what: Sub-50 ms latency on a single workstation GPU makes per-request decisioning feasible in real-time paths.

insights.claim: Most listed decision models are Apache 2.0 licensed (Julia-1, Laya, Kev-4B, lev), while the largest and only image-capable one, OpenJev, is CC BY-NC 4.0, restricting commercial use.
insights.speaker: Xuan-Son Nguyen
insights.so_what: Commercial users needing vision must look elsewhere or negotiate; permissive small models are the deployable default.

insights.claim: Decision models are built on both encoder backbones (mmBERT-small, ModernBERT-large) and Qwen decoder bases (Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.8-27B), showing the category is not tied to one architecture.
insights.speaker: Xuan-Son Nguyen
insights.so_what: Qwen remains a common base for open derivative models; encoders are returning for classification tasks.

insights.claim: New open decision models are appearing weekly, and the llama.cpp team plans to keep adding the best ones, with Cloudflare's Clef next.
insights.speaker: Xuan-Son Nguyen
insights.so_what: Incumbent infrastructure vendors like Cloudflare are entering the category; expect a crowded open field.
insights.quote: New open decision models come out every week

insights.claim: The endpoint supports three question types: choice (top option plus probability per option), score (2 to 10 ordered levels returning an expected level that can fall between two), and noul (yes/no returning probability of yes).
insights.speaker: Xuan-Son Nguyen
insights.so_what: Calibrated probabilities enable threshold-based automation instead of brittle text parsing.

insights.claim: OpenJev can read images such as documents or screenshots, the vision projector downloads automatically, and state can also be a list of chat messages with image_url parts treated as in chat completions.
insights.speaker: Xuan-Son Nguyen
insights.so_what: Document triage (invoice, receipt, contract) can run locally, relevant to back-office automation.

insights.claim: In router mode llama.cpp loads decision models on demand and the caller picks one per request, so multiple models can share one server.
insights.speaker: Xuan-Son Nguyen
insights.so_what: Simplifies deploying a small-model fleet on one box.

insights.claim: Option descriptions materially change decision-model results: Julia-1 routed 'I was charged twice' to shipping with bare labels but to billing at 0.99 once each option was described.
insights.speaker: Xuan-Son Nguyen
insights.so_what: Prompt-like option design still drives accuracy in small models; evaluate with descriptions.
insights.quote: Julia-1 routed "I was charged twice" to shipping with bare labels

insights.claim: Confidence cutoffs must be set per model because calibration differs: a vague ticket scored 0.25 with Julia-1 but 0.80 with Kev-4B.
insights.speaker: Xuan-Son Nguyen
insights.so_what: Human-in-the-loop escalation thresholds are not portable across models; budget for per-model evaluation.
insights.quote: The right cutoff depends on the model

insights.claim: A common pattern is to act automatically on confident answers and send the rest to a human.
insights.speaker: Xuan-Son Nguyen
insights.so_what: Confidence scoring is the mechanism that makes partial automation of support workflows viable.

insights.claim: Questions in one request are answered independently, and Kev-4B, lev and OpenJev process the state only once for all questions, so batching questions amortizes cost.
insights.speaker: Xuan-Son Nguyen
insights.so_what: Batching lowers per-question compute for multi-label workflows.

insights.claim: The decision models ship as GGUF in several quantizations (for example Q8_0), and a community Decision Index compares them, so users are advised to try several sizes because small models are faster and large ones know more.
insights.speaker: Xuan-Son Nguyen
insights.so_what: A community benchmark is emerging as the comparison venue for this category.
